unesco.title: Orteke, traditional performing art in Kazakhstan: dance, puppet and music
unesco.description: Orteke is an indigenous Kazakh performing art that combines theatre, music and puppetry. This folk art entails a music performance with a dombyra, a traditional two-stringed instrument, and a dance performed by a wooden puppet. Attached to the surface of a traditional drum with a metal rod, a wooden puppet in the shape of a mountain goat is connected to the fingers of a musician by one or several strings. As the musician strikes their fingers to play the dombyra, the puppet comes to life, hopping in sync with the music while tapping a rhythmic beat on the drum. Some experts can play with three or more puppets at a time. This performance, fascinating for its simplicity, is enjoyed by children and adults alike. It is primarily transmitted within communities and through apprenticeships, although the Kokil Musical College in Almaty has also established a team of researchers dedicated to the art. The biennial Orteke international festivals and regional puppet art competitions are other platforms for the learning and sharing of skills and experience between puppet artists from Kazakhstan and neighbouring countries. An important part of the region’s folk heritage and identity, Orteke also serves as a communication tool between adults and children.

profile.name: orteke
profile.tagline: A mountain goat marionette dances upon a drum, tethered to a dombra player's striking hand.
profile.insight: In 1935, Kazakh composer Akhmet Zhubanov documented orteke, where a carved goat puppet tied to a musician's fingers frantically leaps across a drumskin in sync with the pluck of a two-stringed dombra.
profile.profile: Orteke is an indigenous Kazakh performing art that fuses traditional string music, percussive puppetry, and rhythmic animal dance. Originating among nomadic pastoralists in southwestern Kazakhstan, the tradition features a seated musician known as a küyshi playing the two-stringed dombra or dombyra. Strings and rods run from the player's fingers or wrists to an articulated wooden figure of a horned mountain goat, which hops and strikes a dauylpaz drum with each plucking gesture. Historically associated with shamanic healing and pastoral observation of wild mountain goats, the art form is maintained today through apprenticeships, college research in Almaty, and international festivals.
profile.profile_long:
Orteke occupies a unique intersection of musical virtuosity, kinetic mimicry, and mechanical puppetry developed among the nomadic communities of Central Asia. Originating in southwestern Kazakhstan and shared across Turkic pastoral traditions, the art form takes its name from the compound of 'or' (meaning a pit, ditch, or trap) and 'teke' (meaning a buck or mountain goat). Ethnomusicologists and folklorists trace its conceptual roots deep into ancient nomadic life, with some scholars proposing that the apparatus originally functioned as a shamanic device designed to captivate wandering spirits or serve as a spirit vessel during healing rituals. Despite these deep roots, the art began to spread more widely in the nineteenth century, eventually entering urban stages when it was staged at the Almaty Puppet Theatre during the 1930s. In 1935, prominent composer and musicologist Akhmet Zhubanov documented the intricate mechanics and cultural role of orteke in an article for Kazakhstanskaya Pravda, securing its place in the formal history of Kazakh national performing arts.

The mechanical choreography of orteke relies entirely on the direct physical link between the instrumentalist—known as a küyshi—and the articulated figurine. As the küyshi sits cross-legged or upright to perform on the dombra (a traditional two-stringed plucked lute), thin cords or threads extend from their fingers, wrists, or feet to the puppet. The puppet itself is mounted above a sounding surface, traditionally a dauylpaz drum or a wooden table draped in animal hide or embroidered textile, held by a metal rod or vertical post. When the musician's right hand plucks, strums, and taps the strings of the dombra, the tension pulls the puppet's hinged limbs, causing the goat to hop, kick, and leap upon the drum membrane. The movement visually mimics a wild mountain goat frantically attempting to leap free from a hunting pit, generating a simultaneous percussive accompaniment that underscores the melodic küy. Highly skilled masters can coordinate multiple puppets simultaneously using intricate manipulations across both hands and feet, occasionally layering wind instruments such as the sazsyrnay clay whistle or the shankobyz jaw harp.

The physical craft of the puppets reflects regional variations and local natural resources across Kazakhstan. In the Semirechye region, artisans traditionally used mountain goat skin, flaying and drying the hide before stuffing it with straw to produce a lightweight, realistic figure. More commonly, craftsmen carve the figures out of local hardwoods, including red birch, walnut, maple, ash, or oak. While the archetypal figure is the horned mountain goat, puppets occasionally take human forms or represent other fauna. The visual presentation is anchored by the instrument and the tabletop stage, often framed by nomadic embroidered patterns that provide contrast against the polished wood and taut hide of the dauylpaz.

Throughout the twentieth century, the tradition weathered profound structural disruptions under Soviet cultural policies, slipping into near-extinction outside rural circles. A turning point occurred in 1984 when orteke was integrated into the national instruments program Murager, revitalizing public interest in heritage instruments. Since 2010, modern Kazakh ensembles such as Er-Turan and Hassak have brought the art form back to prominent domestic and international concert stages. Educational institutions have also stepped in to formalize transmission; while the tradition historically passed entirely from master to apprentice, the Kokil Musical College in Almaty has established dedicated academic research teams. The biennial Orteke International Festival and regional competitions provide regular meeting grounds where masters demonstrate virtuosic puppetry, reinforcing intergenerational ties and providing a vital pedagogical tool that connects elder storytellers with children across Central Asia.

sections.origins_and_history: Orteke originated in southwestern Kazakhstan and spread across Central Asian nomadic pastoral cultures, including regions of Uzbekistan. The name joins 'or' (a ditch, hole, or pit trap) with 'teke' (a buck or male mountain goat). Scholars and ethnographers argue that the practice originated in prehistory, potentially serving ancient shamans as a tool to distract spirits or act as a spirit vessel during therapeutic and healing rites. Although the craft holds ancient roots among Turkic tribes, wider distribution occurred during the nineteenth century. In the 1930s, the performance was presented at the Almaty Puppet Theatre, and in 1935 composer Akhmet Zhubanov published a detailed account in Kazakhstanskaya Pravda. In 1984, the inclusion of orteke in the Murager state cultural program helped rescue the practice from Soviet-era obscurity.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The kinetic dance of orteke is performed not by human bodies stepping across a floor, but by mechanical proxy through an articulated puppet operated by a seated musician. The instrumentalist, known as a küyshi, sits holding a two-stringed dombra. Strings or threads are fastened to the musician's playing fingers or wrists and run to the puppet, which is mounted on a metal rod over a dauylpaz drum or table. As the musician executes rhythmic strumming, finger-striking, and plucking on the instrument, the tension on the strings jerks the puppet's hinged legs. The puppet hops, kicks, and taps the surface in strict synchrony with the musical tempo. The movement intentionally mimics the frantic, agile jumping of a wild mountain goat trying to leap out of a pit. Advanced masters manipulate multiple figurines at once using both hands and feet, adding intricate percussive accents to the performance.
sections.music_and_instruments: The musical foundation of orteke is provided by the dombra (or dombyra), the traditional two-stringed Kazakh long-necked plucked lute. The sound of the plucked strings is acoustically doubled by the percussive impact of the wooden goat striking the skin of a dauylpaz drum, functioning as an integrated self-accompanying percussion system. Virtuosic performers expand the musical palette by incorporating wind instruments such as the sazsyrnay (a traditional clay ocarina) or the shankobyz (jaw harp). The repertoire consists of instrumental küy compositions, historically composed and performed by renowned küyshis including Tattimbet, Bayserke, Shashubay, and Nawryzbay. Performances are entirely instrumental and devoid of spoken dialogue, focusing on the dynamic acoustic dialogue between lute strings and goat-hoof taps.
sections.costume_and_setting: Performances occur in intimate or theatrical indoor and outdoor gathering spaces. The physical apparatus rests upon a wooden table draped with traditional animal skin or fabric decorated with national Kazakh embroidery. The puppet, historically assembled from dried mountain goat skin stuffed with straw in the Semirechye region, is more universally carved from red birch, walnut, maple, ash, or oak wood. The animal features curved horns and flexible joints attached via strings to the performer's digits, mounted firmly above a drum surface via a metal rod. The küyshi typically wears traditional Kazakh dress suited for formal instrumental concerts and community festivals.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Traditionally staged within nomadic encampments and domestic gatherings, orteke serves as an artistic tribute to wildlife, pastoral life, and the rugged mountain ecology inhabited by wild goats. Beyond its historical associations with shamanic healing, the performance functions as an entertaining and educational medium of communication between adults and children. In modern times, orteke is presented at community celebrations, national holiday concerts, the biennial Orteke International Festival, and regional puppetry competitions.
sections.notable_figures: Key historical figures linked to the master repertoire of orteke melodies include classical küyshis Tattimbet, Bayserke, Shashubay, and Nawryzbay. In 1935, Kazakh composer and academic Akhmet Kuanovich Zhubanov provided the first detailed modern analysis of the art form. In the contemporary revival, the musical ensembles Er-Turan and Hassak have brought orteke to international attention, while educators and researchers at the Kokil Musical College in Almaty have led academic documentation and training.
sections.regional_variants: Within Kazakhstan, construction methods vary regionally; the Semirechye region historically utilized real goat hide filled with straw, while western and central regions favoured carved timber from birch, walnut, ash, and oak. Across Central Asia, cognate traditions exist among neighbouring nomadic cultures. In Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and northern Afghanistan, an analogous goat-and-lute puppetry performance is known as buz-bazi. In Kyrgyzstan, the related tradition is termed takteke, which typically features two carved puppets engaged in a simulated combat upon a sounding box, accompanied by the three-stringed komuz.
sections.lineage: Orteke descends from ancient Turkic pastoral puppetry and shamanic performance traditions. During the twentieth century, it transitioned through Soviet folklore programs, including the 1984 Murager national registry. It belongs to the broader Central Asian nomadic family of mechanical puppetry traditions alongside Kyrgyz takteke and Afghan buz-bazi, with lineage preserved today through master-apprentice lineages, academic research at Almaty's Kokil Musical College, and festival competitions.

profile.sacred_note: Ethnographers note ancient historical roots as a shamanic spirit vessel or ritual healing distraction, but the living tradition is secular folk puppetry and music.

basic_steps: not described in sources (performer is seated and manipulates puppet through stringed finger strokes)
teaching.rhythm: Rhythmic accompaniment driven by the plucking pattern of the dombra and the tapping hoofbeats of the puppet upon the dauylpaz drum head.
teaching.formation: Solo instrumentalist seated behind a low table or drum support facing the audience.
teaching.level_notes: Mastery requires simultaneous competence in rapid two-stringed dombra fingerwork and kinetic coordination of tension strings controlling the puppet.

music_profile.vocal_style: instrumental only (dialogues and singing are absent)
music_profile.sound_description: A rapid, resonant plucked lute melody played on the two strings of the dombra, accented by the sharp, intermittent woody clatter and dull tapping of the marionette's hooves landing upon the skin of a dauylpaz drum, occasionally supplemented by the high whistle of the sazsyrnay or the buzzing hum of the shankobyz.

movement_profile.posture: Musician sits upright or cross-legged, holding the dombra steady while arms and hands maintain precise tension over the puppet's connecting cords.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Right plucking hand strikes the dombra strings while fingers and wrists flex upward to pull the puppet's attached strings; expert players incorporate left-hand or foot string tethers.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Musician's torso remains relatively steady to anchor the lute and provide leverage for the puppet's string mechanisms.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Stationary seated stage performance focused on a small tabletop or drumhead area.
movement_profile.partnering: Solo performance; partnering exists purely between human musician and mechanical puppet.
movement_profile.tempo_feel: Energetic, agile, and syncopated, reflecting the startled jumps of a trapped mountain goat.

signature_moves.name: goat leaping
signature_moves.description: The rapid jumping and hopping of the puppet across the drum skin driven by finger plucking gestures.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: The wooden puppet performs continuous small hops, vertical leaps, and landing strikes upon the drumhead.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid slackening the control cords, which disrupts the simultaneous rhythm between the dombra notes and the drum taps.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Wooden Goat That Dances on a Drum
episode_brief.logline: A Kazakh dombra master shows how ancient nomadic hunters turned music into kinetic magic with a dancing mountain goat puppet tied directly to his fingertips.
beats: Close-up on a two-stringed dombra neck in Almaty as fingers pluck a rapid küy melody.
The camera pans down a taught thread to reveal a hand-carved wooden goat leaping on a dauylpaz drum head.
Archival exploration of Akhmet Zhubanov's 1935 article describing the nomadic hunting origin—the teke trying to leap from a pit trap.
Workshop visit showing the carving of birch wood and the balancing of straw and goat hide in the Semirechye style.
Classroom scene at the Kokil Musical College in Almaty where young apprentices practice plucking while managing string tension.
Performance demonstration by ensemble members of Hassak demonstrating advanced multi-puppet control using hands and feet.
Final crescendo as the puppet strikes a flurry of drum taps in sync with the song's ending chord.

lesson_ladder.goal: Grasp the mechanical concept of orteke by linking finger motion to puppet movement.
drills: Practice steady open-string dombra strumming without puppet attachment.
Attach a single cord to the middle finger and practice lifting the digit to lift an object vertically.
Synchronize a single string-pluck with a downward landing of the tethered puppet.

lesson_ladder.goal: Coordinate a basic küy rhythm with sustained rhythmic drum taps.
drills: Execute basic melodic küy patterns while keeping cord tension consistent.
Control puppet rebound on the dauylpaz drum skin to avoid double bounces.
Maintain clear tempo while switching between plucking strokes.

lesson_ladder.goal: Advanced multi-puppet or wind accompaniment coordination.
drills: Coordinate two puppets attached to separate fingers of the right and left hands.
Integrate foot-pedal cords to trigger auxiliary jumping movements.
Combine dombra and puppet play with brief shankobyz or sazsyrnay interludes.

visual_motifs: Carved wooden goat horns silhouette against stage lights
Vibrating dombra strings alongside taut tether lines
Close-up of hooves impacting the hide of the dauylpaz drum
Traditional Kazakh national embroidery on table coverings
episode_brief.instructor_persona: A patient, master küyshi and instrument maker from Almaty who combines deep technical discipline on the dombra with whimsical storytelling.
episode_brief.music_cue: A brisk traditional küy composed by Tattimbet or Bayserke, driven by fast dombra strumming and punctuated by rhythmic wooden drum taps.

connections.name: buz-bazi
connections.note: Shared tradition of goat-and-lute mechanical puppetry practiced in Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Afghanistan.

connections.name: takteke
connections.note: Kyrgyz tradition where two combatant puppets are manipulated alongside the playing of the komuz.

gaps: Specific metronome markings (BPM) and metrical signatures for standard orteke melodies are not specified in the sources.
Specific choreographic human footwork counts are not described because human dancers do not dance; the dance is performed by the puppet.

claims.text: Orteke is a traditional performing art originating in Kazakhstan combining puppetry, music, and dance.
claims.quote: Orteke (Kazakh: ортеке) is a form of traditional performance in Kazakhstan that incorporates puppetry, music, and dance.

claims.text: The name orteke unites terms meaning pit or trap and goat.
claims.quote: The name "orteke" combines or (ditch, hole, trap) and teke (goat).

claims.text: The performance features a wooden puppet connected by cords to a musician playing the two-stringed dombra.
claims.quote: In orteke, a musician playing a two-stringed dombra has a wooden puppet attached to their fingers by sticks and strings.

claims.text: The puppet hops over a drum such as the dauylpaz, tapping out an audible rhythmic beat.
claims.quote: The puppet, usually shaped like a horned mountain goat, is attached to the top of a drum, often a dauylpaz. As the musician plays, the puppet moves to the rhythm, creating a drumbeat.

claims.text: Some scholars propose orteke originated as a shamanic device used in spirit distraction or healing rites.
claims.quote: Some ethnographers argue the Orteke began as a shamanic tool to distract spirits or to act as a "spirit vessel" during healing rituals.

claims.text: Composer Akhmet Zhubanov published a detailed account of orteke in Kazakhstanskaya Pravda in 1935.
claims.quote: Nel 1935 il compositore Achmet Kuanovič Žubanov descrisse in dettaglio l'orteke in un articolo della Kazachstanskaja pravda.

claims.text: In the Semirechye region, puppets were made from flayed mountain goat skin stuffed with straw.
claims.quote: Ad esempio nell'oblast' di Semireč'e viene utilizzata la pelle delle capre di montagna, che viene scuoiata, essiccata e riempita con paglia.

claims.text: Orteke performances do not include spoken dialogue.
claims.quote: Gli spettacoli sono accompagnati da musica e i dialoghi sono assenti.

claims.text: The puppet's erratic jumping represents a wild mountain goat attempting to scramble out of a pit trap.
claims.quote: ricordano il tentativo di uscire dalla fossa in cui esso è caduto, imitando appunto le capre selvatiche di montagna.

claims.text: In 1984, orteke was integrated into the Murager program, renewing its popularity after years of Soviet neglect.
claims.quote: Nel 1984 l'orteke venne inserito all'interno della lista degli strumenti nazionali del programma "Murager" e tornò a godere di popolarità dopo anni di dominio sovietico.

claims.text: The Kokil Musical College in Almaty operates a research group devoted to studying the art.
claims.quote: the Kokil Musical College in Almaty has also established a team of researchers dedicated to the art.
